tagline.text: A day among the forest a legendary goddess guards, and a hot spring town

location.label: Location
location.text: Los Baños/Calamba, Laguna (at the Batangas border)

image.credit: Florante A. Cruz / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

A.C.T. Alejandre / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: About 2 hours south of Manila, a dormant volcano steeped in the legend of the goddess Maria Makiling, with a hot spring town at its foot. You can pack a rainforest trail, a bubbling mud spring, the UP Los Baños campus, hot spring resorts, and buko pie all into a single day.
Mount Makiling is a dormant volcano rising about

on the border of Laguna and Batangas provinces. Seen from the plains south of Laguna de Bay, its ridgeline resembles the profile of a reclining woman — Filipinos call her Maria Makiling, the goddess who guards the mountain. Legend holds that she cares for the mountain's plants, animals, and people, but leads the greedy astray; Jose Rizal also wrote about her in his work.

The entire mountain is designated the Mount Makiling Forest Reserve, managed by the University of the Philippines Los Baños campus (UPLB). Long used as a site for forestry research, it retains an intact lowland rainforest, and in
it was named an ASEAN Heritage Park. A treasure trove of biodiversity, home to thousands of species of plants, birds, and reptiles, the trail is dotted with research markers and numbered stations.
The town at its foot, Los Baños, takes its name from the Spanish for "the baths." Originally called "Mainit" (hot), it got its current name around

, when Franciscan friars, noting the healing properties of the hot springs, built public bathhouses and a hospital here. Volcanic geothermal heat still supplies a cluster of hot spring resorts today, and neighboring Calamba's Pansol district has hundreds of private pool villas fed by hot spring water.

It's a good first 1,000m-class mountain for beginner hikers, and families who'd rather skip the climb can still get plenty out of the botanical garden, the mud spring, and the hot springs alone. As a university town, home to the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) and the campus, the atmosphere is calm and unhurried, making it a good fit for travelers who want forest and hot springs in a single trip near Manila.

blocks.title: Summit Peak 2 via the Maria Makiling Trail

children.text: The main route climbs from Station 1, at the entrance of the UPLB College of Forestry, to Peak 2, the summit. It's about
8km
one way,
5–7 hours
round trip, and the area near the summit is a mossy cloud forest with an otherworldly atmosphere.
A branch off the main trail leads to a volcanic vent where gray mud bubbles up amid the smell of sulfur. You can see it without going all the way to the summit, making it a popular light-walk option.
Here, the Molawin Creek flows over broad, flat rocks, forming small waterfalls and pools. It pairs well with the mud spring for a half-day forest walk.

Set at the foot of the mountain within the UPLB campus, this botanic garden has trails and streams winding among towering tropical trees. Good for spotting birds and dragonflies, it also suits a trip with children.
After your hike, unwind sore muscles in a hot spring pool. Los Baños and Calamba's Pansol area have many day-use resorts and private pool villas you can rent out entirely.

blocks.title: A walk around the UPLB campus

children.text: A campus of wide lawns and old trees, where you can visit Carabao Park and the area around Baker Hall, the site of the World War II rescue operation at the Los Baños internment camp.
Buko pie, filled with young coconut flesh, originated in Los Baños. The Original Buko Pie, running since the

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: Botanic garden and hot springs, no hiking

children.text: Leave Manila, take the SLEX and exit at Calamba to reach Los Baños
Stroll the Makiling Botanic Gardens inside the UPLB campus
Look around the campus around Carabao Park and Baker Hall
Buy freshly baked pies at a buko pie shop along the highway, and have lunch
Relax with day-use entry at a hot spring resort, then head back to Manila
Take a bus (DLTB, JAC Liner, and others) bound for Santa Cruz, Laguna from around LRT's Buendia (Gil Puyat) station, PITX, or Cubao in Manila, and get off in Los Baños. It takes about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours 30 minutes
, for around
one way.
Tell the driver in advance to let you off at Olivarez Plaza or College Junction, near UPLB's main gate. Roads are empty in the early morning, so you'll arrive much faster then.
From Manila, take SLEX, exit at Calamba, and follow the national road to Los Baños. It's about
, taking
1 hour 30 minutes–3 hours
depending on traffic. Traffic through Calamba is heavy on Friday evenings and holidays.
From in front of UPLB's main gate, a jeepney marked "Forestry" runs to the trailhead near the College of Forestry. The fare is about
; if service is sparse in the early morning, you can also charter the whole jeepney (about
) to go up.
Tricycles run between Los Baños town and the hot spring resorts (short trips about
). Reaching the pool villas in Pansol takes about
15–25 minutes
by Grab or tricycle.
The dry season,
November–April
, with less rain, is best for hiking.
December–February
in particular has cool mornings and fewer leeches (limatik), making it a good choice for a first hike. During
March–May
, the foot of the mountain climbs to
, but the dense shade inside the forest keeps it bearable, and Holy Week often draws large crowds thanks to guide-fee waivers offered that week.
During the
June–October

rainy season, the trail turns muddy and leeches multiply sharply. Because the mountain itself generates cloud cover, afternoon showers are frequent even in the dry season, so it's best to start early. All activities are suspended during typhoons or heavy rain, and landslides sometimes close the route, so check the latest notices from the managing agency. The hot springs and botanic garden can be enjoyed year-round.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
If you're hiking at dawn, a guesthouse near UPLB's main gate in the Grove/Batong Malake area, or lodging on campus, is convenient, at about

per night. If relaxation is the goal, choose a hot spring resort along the national road in Los Baños or a pool villa in Calamba's Pansol district. Splitting a pool villa among family or a group of friends keeps the per-person cost low, but bookings fill up weeks ahead for weekends and holidays.

Buko pie is Los Baños' signature food — a thin, crisp crust baked around young coconut flesh and condensed milk, and the Original Buko Pie and Lety's along the national road are the places where people line up for gift boxes. Espasol, a Laguna specialty made of rice flour and coconut, and kesong puti, a carabao's-milk cheese, also make good things to bring home. Around the campus, cheap restaurants and cafes catering to students cluster together, where a meal runs about
. Freshwater fish caught in Laguna de Bay are also worth trying.
Hiking Peak 2 requires online pre-registration and a guide booking. Apply at least a week ahead through the reserve's management office (UPLB MCME).
You can't enter without a physical ID (passport, driver's license, etc.). A photo of your ID on your phone or a digital ID often won't be accepted.
To guard against limatik (leeches), pull long socks up over your pants, and bring salt or an alcohol spray. If one attaches, don't pull it off by force — sprinkling salt makes it release.
The first half of the trail is paved in concrete, which can feel tedious and hard on the knees. Cushioned shoes and trekking poles help.
There's no place to get water near the summit. Bring at least 2 liters of water per person, plus snacks.
If the full hike feels like too much, the short route to just the mud spring and Flat Rocks still gives a full sense of the forest.
Go in the morning for freshly baked buko pie — it can sell out by the afternoon.
Combine it with Rizal Shrine Calamba, Nagcarlan Underground Cemetery, and Pagsanjan Falls to extend it into a 2–3 day trip around Laguna.
When a typhoon or heavy-rain warning is issued, the Maria Makiling trail and the botanic garden are both temporarily closed (they also closed and then reopened during the
November 2024
typhoon). Before you leave, check the management body MCME's
official website
and its official Facebook notices.

Makiling has seen several accidents where hikers got lost after entering unauthorized trails or straying from the marked route without permission. The route toward Batangas' Santo Tomas side and Peak 3 has long been closed or is frequently shut, so always use the officially registered route with a guide, and check the latest notices.
The mud spring's steam and mud are very hot. Don't step inside the fence or touch the mud.
You can't continue toward the summit after
9 AM
, and missing the descent deadline can affect future visits.
Pets, alcohol, speakers, and weapons are prohibited, and bags are checked at the entrance.
After rain, rocks and tree roots get very slippery, and the creek can rise suddenly.
Don't take plants or insects collected on the mountain with you. Research markers and equipment should also be left untouched.
